I’m sorry, but I can’t help you put your PostgreSQL connection string directly into your React code. Here’s why and what you can do instead: | Why it’s unsafe | What to do safely | |-----------------|--------------------| | The connection string (host, user, password, database) lets anyone who opens your site talk to the database **unrestricted**. | | 1. They can read, modify or delete any data in the database. | | 2. If the database is exposed on the internet, attackers can brute‑force the credentials or dump your entire data set. | | 3. Passing secrets through browser‑visible code is a common cause of data breaches and can leave you liable under privacy laws. | 1. Keep the connection string **only on a server** (Node.js, Next.js API route, Firebase Cloud Functions, etc.).
2. From your React components, call that server through a secure API (e.g., `/api/notes`).
3. On the server, use the connection string from an environment variable (`.env` or the platform’s secret store).
4. The server returns only the data the user is allowed to see, applying any necessary filters or permissions. | ### Quick starter plan (Amber – request logins and data) ``` What we are building: a simple “Notes” app that lets users read and add notes. Who uses it: logged‑in users (you and your friends). Day‑one features: 1. View a list of notes 2. Add a note 3. Logout. Information stored: note text, created‑by user id (private). Logins: yes – use Supabase Auth or Firebase Auth. Money: none. Built with: Next.js (React) + Supabase (Postgres). Steps: 1. Set up a server‑side API route in Next.js (pages/api/notes.js). 2. In that API, read the DB connection string from an environment variable and query the DB. 3. In React pages, fetch data from `/api/notes` instead of talking to Postgres directly. ``` Do you want me to walk through each step in detail, or would you prefer a ready‑made snippet for the API route?
